claim: Piezo1 is expressed in the interdigit region of embryonic limb buds at E12.5 to E14.5.
source: At E12.5 to E14.5, when endochondral bone initiates, we found by whole mount in situ hybridization (WISH) that Piezo1 is mostly expressed in the interdigit region while Piezo2 is expressed in the forming digit and wrist (Figure 1a, Figure 1—figure supplement 1a,b).
evidence: Supported by whole mount in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 1a and supplementary figures.

claim: Piezo2 is expressed in the forming digit and wrist of embryonic limb buds at E12.5 to E14.5.
source: At E12.5 to E14.5, when endochondral bone initiates, we found by whole mount in situ hybridization (WISH) that Piezo1 is mostly expressed in the interdigit region while Piezo2 is expressed in the forming digit and wrist (Figure 1a, Figure 1—figure supplement 1a,b).
evidence: Supported by whole mount in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 1a and supplementary figures.

claim: Piezo1 is expressed in differentiating osteoblast cells in the perichondrium and periosteum.
source: Piezo1 was most strongly expressed in the connective tissues associated with the muscle and weaker expression of Piezo1 expression was detected in the muscle and differentiating osteoblast cells in the perichondrium and periosteum (Figure 1—figure supplement 1c).
evidence: Supported by in situ hybridization data using RNAscope technology shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1c.

claim: Piezo1 protein is detected in connective tissue, muscle, and differentiating osteoblast cells expressing Osterix at E13.5, E15.5, and P0.
source: Consistent with the in situ hybridization data (Figure 1—figure supplement 1c), Piezo1 protein was detected in the connective tissue, the associated muscle and differentiating osteoblast cells that express Osterix (Sp7) in the perichondrium and periosteum at E13.5, E15.5 and postnatal day 0 (P0) neonatal pups (Figure 1b,c).
evidence: Supported by immunostaining data from Piezo1P1-tdT mice shown in Figure 1b,c.

claim: Piezo1 is expressed in hypertrophic chondrocytes, tendons, and ligaments.
source: Piezo1 expression was also detected in the hypertrophic chondrocytes, tendons and ligaments (Figure 1b,c).
evidence: Supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 1b,c.

claim: Piezo2 lineage cells include Sp7+ osteoblast cells, joint cells, sporadic growth plate chondrocytes, tendons, and connective tissue cells in muscle.
source: The tdTomato+ Piezo2 lineage cells (Piezo2+ cells and their descendants) included Sp7+ osteoblast cells, joint cells, sporadic growth plate chondrocytes, tendons and connective tissue cells in the muscle (Figure 1d, Figure 1—figure supplement 1d,e).
evidence: Supported by lineage tracing data from Piezo2EGFP-Cre crossed with Rosa-tdTomato reporter mice shown in Figure 1d and supplementary figures.

claim: Piezo1 CKO mice exhibit multiple bone fractures in radius and ulna at birth.
source: However, the Piezo1 CKO mice exhibited multiple bone fractures in radius and ulna suggesting severely reduced bone formation (Figure 2a).
evidence: Supported by skeletal staining data shown in Figure 2a.

claim: Piezo2 CKO mice exhibit grossly normal skeletal development with no bone fracture.
source: The Piezo2 CKO mice exhibited grossly normal skeletal development with no bone fracture, but the Piezo1/2 double conditional (Piezo1/2 DKO) mutant mice demonstrated more severe skeletal defects including additional fractures in the femur (Figure 2a,b, Figure 2—source data 1, Figure 2—figure supplement 1a, Figure 2—figure supplement 1—source data 1).
evidence: Supported by skeletal staining and μCT data shown in Figure 2a,b and supplementary figures.

claim: Piezo1/2 DKO mutant mice demonstrate more severe skeletal defects including additional fractures in the femur.
source: The Piezo2 CKO mice exhibited grossly normal skeletal development with no bone fracture, but the Piezo1/2 double conditional (Piezo1/2 DKO) mutant mice demonstrated more severe skeletal defects including additional fractures in the femur (Figure 2a,b, Figure 2—source data 1, Figure 2—figure supplement 1a, Figure 2—figure supplement 1—source data 1).
evidence: Supported by skeletal staining and μCT data shown in Figure 2a,b and supplementary figures.

claim: Long bones are shortened in the absence of Piezo1.
source: We also found that long bones were shortened in the absence of Piezo1, but not Piezo 2, and further shortening was observed in the Piezo1/2 DKO mutants (Figure 2b).
evidence: Supported by μCT measurements shown in Figure 2b.

claim: Long bones are not shortened in the absence of Piezo2 alone.
source: We also found that long bones were shortened in the absence of Piezo1, but not Piezo 2, and further shortening was observed in the Piezo1/2 DKO mutants (Figure 2b).
evidence: Supported by μCT measurements shown in Figure 2b.

claim: Further shortening of long bones is observed in Piezo1/2 DKO mutants.
source: We also found that long bones were shortened in the absence of Piezo1, but not Piezo 2, and further shortening was observed in the Piezo1/2 DKO mutants (Figure 2b).
evidence: Supported by μCT measurements shown in Figure 2b.

claim: Piezo1 plays a major role while Piezo2 shares some redundant functions with Piezo1 in mesenchymal progenitor cells during skeletal development.
source: These results indicate that while Piezo1 plays a major role, Piezo2 shares some of the Piezo1 functions in mesenchymal progenitor cells during skeletal development.
evidence: Inferred from the differential severity of skeletal phenotypes in Piezo1 CKO, Piezo2 CKO, and Piezo1/2 DKO mice.

claim: Piezo1 expression is progressively increased in young mice postnatally.
source: Mechanical stress increases postnatally and we found that Piezo1 expression was progressively increased in young mice (Figure 2—figure supplement 1b), suggesting that Piezo1 also regulates bone formation after birth in adult lives.
evidence: Supported by Western blotting and RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1b.

claim: Piezo2 mRNA expression is reduced in postnatal mice in the cortical bone.
source: However, Piezo2 mRNA expression was reduced in postnatal mice in the cortical bone (Figure 2—figure supplement 1b).
evidence: Supported by RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1b.

claim: Both cortical and trabecular bone masses are reduced in Piezo1 CKO mice at P21.
source: The μCT analyses showed that both cortical and trabecular bone masses were reduced in the Piezo1 CKO mice and further reduced in the Piezo1/2 DKO mice at the age of P21.
evidence: Supported by μCT data shown in Figure 2c,d.

claim: Cortical and trabecular bone masses are further reduced in Piezo1/2 DKO mice at P21.
source: The μCT analyses showed that both cortical and trabecular bone masses were reduced in the Piezo1 CKO mice and further reduced in the Piezo1/2 DKO mice at the age of P21.
evidence: Supported by μCT data shown in Figure 2c,d.

claim: Piezo2 CKO mice exhibit normal bone mass at P21.
source: The Piezo2 CKO mice exhibited normal bone mass (Figure 2c,d, Figure 2—source data 1).
evidence: Supported by μCT data shown in Figure 2c,d.

claim: Reduction of collagens in trabecular and cortical bones is observed in P5 Piezo1 CKO and Piezo1/2 DKO mutant pups.
source: Analyses of postnatal bone development of Piezo1/2 mutant pups were performed by Masson's Trichrome staining, which showed reduction of collagens in the trabecular and cortical bones of the P5 Piezo1 CKO and Piezo1/2 DKO mutant pups (Figure 2—figure supplement 1c).
evidence: Supported by Masson's Trichrome staining data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1c.

claim: Serum PINP levels are reduced in Piezo1 CKO and Piezo1/2 DKO mice.
source: Bone formation was definitively examined by ELISA assays of serum procollagen type I N propeptide (PINP) levels (Figure 2—figure supplement 1c), which is considered clinically as the most sensitive bone formation marker (Samoszuk et al., 2008).
evidence: Supported by ELISA data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1d.

claim: Mineralization apposition rate (MAR) and bone formation rate (BFR) are reduced in periosteum of cortical bone in Piezo1 CKO mice.
source: Furthermore, histomorphometric analysis showed reduced mineralization apposition rate (MAR), and bone formation rate (BFR) in periosteum of the cortical bone of the Piezo1 CKO mice (Figure 2e, Figure 2—source data 1).
evidence: Supported by histomorphometric analysis data shown in Figure 2e.

claim: Cortical bone formation in Piezo1/2 DKO mice is too severely reduced to allow accurate quantification.
source: Reduction of cortical bone formation in the Piezo1/2 DKO mutant mice or trabecular bone formation in both Piezo1 CKO and Piezo1/2 DKO mice were too severe to allow accurate quantification (Figure 2e,f).
evidence: Supported by histomorphometric analysis data shown in Figure 2e,f.

claim: Trabecular bone formation in both Piezo1 CKO and Piezo1/2 DKO mice is too severely reduced to allow accurate quantification.
source: Reduction of cortical bone formation in the Piezo1/2 DKO mutant mice or trabecular bone formation in both Piezo1 CKO and Piezo1/2 DKO mice were too severe to allow accurate quantification (Figure 2e,f).
evidence: Supported by histomorphometric analysis data shown in Figure 2e,f.

claim: The secondary spongiosa is almost completely missing in Piezo1/2 DKO mice.
source: In the Piezo1/2 DKO mice, the secondary spongiosa was almost completely missing.
evidence: Inferred from histomorphometric analysis data.

claim: Osteoclast marker expression (Ctsk and Acp5) is upregulated in Piezo1 CKO and Piezo1/2 DKO mutant mice.
source: Reduction of bone formation in the Piezo1 CKO and Piezo1/2 DKO mutant mice was accompanied by increase in bone remodeling indicated by upregulated expression of osteoclast markers Cathepsin K (Ctsk) and Tartrate-resistant acid phosphatase (Acp5 or Trap) (Figure 2—figure supplement 1e,f).
evidence: Supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1e,f.

claim: At E16.5, there is no difference in osteoclast marker expression between wild-type and Piezo1/2 mutants.
source: However, earlier in development at E16.5, there was no difference in osteoclast marker expression (data not shown) suggesting that increased osteoclast differentiation may have resulted from the changes in osteoblast cells.
evidence: Supported by unpublished data mentioned in the text.

claim: Early and mature osteoblast marker expression is reduced in Piezo1 CKO and Piezo1/2 DKO mutants at P0.
source: Indeed, quantitative gene expression analysis by qRT-PCR further showed that while early and mature osteoblast marker expression were reduced, Tnfsf11 (Rankl) and Acp5 expression, indicative of osteoclast differentiation, were increased in the Piezo1 CKO and Piezo1/2 DKO mutant at P0 (Figure 2—figure supplement 1g).
evidence: Supported by qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1g.

claim: Tnfsf11 (Rankl) and Acp5 expression is increased in Piezo1 CKO and Piezo1/2 DKO mutants at P0.
source: Indeed, quantitative gene expression analysis by qRT-PCR further showed that while early and mature osteoblast marker expression were reduced, Tnfsf11 (Rankl) and Acp5 expression, indicative of osteoclast differentiation, were increased in the Piezo1 CKO and Piezo1/2 DKO mutant at P0 (Figure 2—figure supplement 1g).
evidence: Supported by qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1g.

claim: Tnfrsf11b (Opg) expression is reduced in Piezo1 CKO and Piezo1/2 DKO mutants.
source: Expression of Tnfrsf11b (Opg), which encodes a decoy receptor of Tnfsf11 to inhibit osteoclast differentiation, was also reduced.
evidence: Inferred from qRT-PCR data.

claim: Reduced bone mass and density in the absence of Piezo channels is a combination of reduced bone formation and increased bone resorption.
source: Therefore, reduced bone mass and density in the absence of Piezo channels is a combination of reduced bone formation and increased bone resorption, which resulted in not only bone fractures, but also reduced longitudinal bone growth and bone deformity such as bowing of the tibia (Figure 2—figure supplement 1a).
evidence: Inferred from multiple experimental data including μCT, histomorphometry, and gene expression analyses.

claim: Expression of Sox9 and Col10a1 is similar in wild-type, Piezo1 CKO, and Piezo1/2 DKO embryos at E16.5 and P0.
source: At E16.5 and P0, expression of the chondrocyte marker Sox9 and hypertrophic chondrocyte marker Col10a1 was similar in the wild-type control, Piezo1 CKO and Piezo1/2 DKO embryos (Figure 3a, Figure 3—figure supplement 1), suggesting cartilage formation and chondrocyte hypertrophy was not regulated by Piezo1/2 in development.
evidence: Supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 3a and Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: Cartilage formation and chondrocyte hypertrophy are not regulated by Piezo1/2 in development.
source: At E16.5 and P0, expression of the chondrocyte marker Sox9 and hypertrophic chondrocyte marker Col10a1 was similar in the wild-type control, Piezo1 CKO and Piezo1/2 DKO embryos (Figure 3a, Figure 3—figure supplement 1), suggesting cartilage formation and chondrocyte hypertrophy was not regulated by Piezo1/2 in development.
evidence: Inferred from similar expression patterns of chondrocyte markers in wild-type and mutant embryos.

claim: Expression of Sp7 is markedly reduced in Piezo1 CKO humerus at E16.5 and P0.
source: However, expression of the early osteoblast marker Sp7 was markedly reduced at E16.5 and P0 in the ossifying regions of the developing Piezo1 CKO humerus and further reduced in the Piezo1/2 DKO humerus (Figure 3a and Figure 3—figure supplement 1), suggesting that Piezo1/2 are required to promote osteoblast differentiation in development.
evidence: Supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 3a and Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: Expression of Sp7 is further reduced in Piezo1/2 DKO humerus at E16.5 and P0.
source: However, expression of the early osteoblast marker Sp7 was markedly reduced at E16.5 and P0 in the ossifying regions of the developing Piezo1 CKO humerus and further reduced in the Piezo1/2 DKO humerus (Figure 3a and Figure 3—figure supplement 1), suggesting that Piezo1/2 are required to promote osteoblast differentiation in development.
evidence: Supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 3a and Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: Piezo1/2 are required to promote osteoblast differentiation in development.
source: However, expression of the early osteoblast marker Sp7 was markedly reduced at E16.5 and P0 in the ossifying regions of the developing Piezo1 CKO humerus and further reduced in the Piezo1/2 DKO humerus (Figure 3a and Figure 3—figure supplement 1), suggesting that Piezo1/2 are required to promote osteoblast differentiation in development.
evidence: Inferred from reduced Sp7 expression in Piezo1/2 mutants.

claim: Bone mineralization is reduced in Piezo1 CKO and Piezo1/2 DKO mutants at P0.
source: Bone mineralization and osteoblast maturation as indicated by von Kossa staining and secreted phosphoprotein 1 (Spp1, also known as Opn) immunofluorescent staining were also reduced in the trabecular and cortical bone areas at P0 (Figure 3d,e).
evidence: Supported by von Kossa staining and Spp1 immunostaining data shown in Figure 3d,e.

claim: Osteoblast maturation is reduced in Piezo1 CKO and Piezo1/2 DKO mutants at P0.
source: Bone mineralization and osteoblast maturation as indicated by von Kossa staining and secreted phosphoprotein 1 (Spp1, also known as Opn) immunofluorescent staining were also reduced in the trabecular and cortical bone areas at P0 (Figure 3d,e).
evidence: Supported by von Kossa staining and Spp1 immunostaining data shown in Figure 3d,e.

claim: Growth plate chondrocyte proliferation is reduced in Piezo1 CKO and further reduced in Piezo1/2 DKO mutants at E16.5.
source: When examined by BrdU labeling, we found that growth plate chondrocyte proliferation and the length of the proliferative regions were both reduced in the Piezo1 CKO and further reduced in the Piezo1/2 DKO mutant at E16.5 (Figure 3b, Figure 3—source data 1).
evidence: Supported by BrdU labeling data shown in Figure 3b.

claim: The length of proliferative regions is reduced in Piezo1 CKO and further reduced in Piezo1/2 DKO mutants at E16.5.
source: When examined by BrdU labeling, we found that growth plate chondrocyte proliferation and the length of the proliferative regions were both reduced in the Piezo1 CKO and further reduced in the Piezo1/2 DKO mutant at E16.5 (Figure 3b, Figure 3—source data 1).
evidence: Supported by BrdU labeling data shown in Figure 3b.

claim: Increased apoptosis is found in the bone and muscle of Piezo1 CKO and Piezo1/2 DKO mutants at E16.5.
source: Increased apoptosis was found in the bone and muscle of the Piezo1 CKO and Piezo1/2 DKO mutant at E16.5 by TUNEL assay (Figure 3c).
evidence: Supported by TUNEL assay data shown in Figure 3c.

claim: Piezo1/2 MS channels are required for cartilage growth and bone formation in embryonic development.
source: These analyses indicate that Piezo1/2 MS channels are required for cartilage growth and bone formation in embryonic development, providing mechanistic insights into findings made in human populations that PIEZO1 SNPs are associated with reduced body height and eBMD (Marouli et al., 2017; Morris et al., 2019).
evidence: Inferred from multiple experimental data and supported by human GWAS studies.

claim: PIEZO1 SNPs are associated with reduced body height in humans.
source: These analyses indicate that Piezo1/2 MS channels are required for cartilage growth and bone formation in embryonic development, providing mechanistic insights into findings made in human populations that PIEZO1 SNPs are associated with reduced body height and eBMD (Marouli et al., 2017; Morris et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citation to human GWAS study.

claim: PIEZO1 SNPs are associated with reduced eBMD in humans.
source: These analyses indicate that Piezo1/2 MS channels are required for cartilage growth and bone formation in embryonic development, providing mechanistic insights into findings made in human populations that PIEZO1 SNPs are associated with reduced body height and eBMD (Marouli et al., 2017; Morris et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citation to human GWAS study.

claim: Sp7-Cre; Piezo1f/f and Sp7-Cre; Piezo1f/f; Piezo2f/f mouse pups do not show limb bone fractures.
source: Interestingly, the Sp7-Cre; Piezo1f/f (Piezo1CKO) and Sp7-Cre; Piezo1f/f; Piezo2f/f (Piezo1/2 DKO) mouse pups did not show limb bone fractures.
evidence: Supported by skeletal analysis data.

claim: Multiple bone fractures are found in the ribs at P21 in Sp7-Cre-driven Piezo1CKO and Piezo1/2 DKO mice.
source: However, multiple bone fractures were found in the ribs at P21 in the Piezo1CKO and Piezo1/2 DKO mice, but not the Piezo2 CKO mice (Figure 4a).
evidence: Supported by skeletal staining data shown in Figure 4a.

claim: Loss of Piezo1 or Piezo1/2 in Sp7+ cells leads to reduced trabecular and cortical bones.
source: μCT analyses showed that loss of Piezo1 or Piezo1/2 in Sp7+ cells led to reduced trabecular and cortical bones (Figure 4b, Supplementary file 1, Source data 1) and Sp7 expression (Figure 4c).
evidence: Supported by μCT data shown in Figure 4b and Supplementary file 1.

claim: Loss of Piezo1 or Piezo1/2 in Sp7+ cells leads to reduced Sp7 expression.
source: μCT analyses showed that loss of Piezo1 or Piezo1/2 in Sp7+ cells led to reduced trabecular and cortical bones (Figure 4b, Supplementary file 1, Source data 1) and Sp7 expression (Figure 4c).
evidence: Supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 4c.

claim: Reduction in bone mass is more severe in Prrx1-Cre-driven mutants compared to Sp7-Cre-driven mutants.
source: Reduction in bone mass was more severe in the Prrx1-Cre-driven mutants compared to the Sp7-Cre-driven ones (Figure 2d and Supplementary file 1), suggesting that Piezo1/2 in Sp7- cells such as the muscle, tenocytes and chondrocytes may also promote to bone formation.
evidence: Supported by comparison of μCT data from different Cre drivers.

claim: Piezo1/2 in Sp7- cells such as muscle, tenocytes, and chondrocytes may also promote bone formation.
source: Reduction in bone mass was more severe in the Prrx1-Cre-driven mutants compared to the Sp7-Cre-driven ones (Figure 2d and Supplementary file 1), suggesting that Piezo1/2 in Sp7- cells such as the muscle, tenocytes and chondrocytes may also promote to bone formation.
evidence: Inferred from comparison of phenotypes between different Cre-driven mutants.

claim: Mechanical stress slightly increases Piezo1 expression in Prrx1 lineage cells but not Sp7 lineage cells.
source: In addition, we found that when cultured under osteogenic conditions, mechanical stress slightly increased Piezo1 expression in the Prrx1 lineage cells, not the Sp7 lineage cells (Figure 4d).
evidence: Supported by RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 4d.

claim: Yoda1 promotes bone formation and osteoblast differentiation in wild-type limbs but not Piezo1/2 DKO limbs in explant culture.
source: However, Yoda1 promoted bone formation and osteoblast differentiation in the wild type, but not the Piezo1/2 DKO limbs (Figure 5a), suggesting that Piezo1 was functional in the explant culture.
evidence: Supported by limb explant culture data shown in Figure 5a.

claim: The drastic difference in bone formation between wild-type and Sp7-Cre; Piezo1/2 DKO limbs developed in utero is eliminated in explant culture.
source: Importantly, the drastic difference in bone formation between the wild-type control and the Sp7-Cre; Piezo1/2 DKO limbs developed in utero was eliminated (compare Figure 5b with Figure 4a,c).
evidence: Supported by comparison of limb explant culture data (Figure 5b) with in vivo data (Figure 4a,c).

claim: BTX injection reduces bone mass in wild-type mice.
source: While BTX injection reduced bone mass in the wild-type mice, in the Sp7-Cre-driven Piezo1/2 DKO mice, BTX injection did not cause significant bone loss, although the bone mass was lower compared to that of the wild-type controls (Figure 5c, Figure 5—source data 1).
evidence: Supported by μCT data from BTX-induced muscle paralysis model shown in Figure 5c.

claim: BTX injection does not cause significant bone loss in Sp7-Cre-driven Piezo1/2 DKO mice.
source: While BTX injection reduced bone mass in the wild-type mice, in the Sp7-Cre-driven Piezo1/2 DKO mice, BTX injection did not cause significant bone loss, although the bone mass was lower compared to that of the wild-type controls (Figure 5c, Figure 5—source data 1).
evidence: Supported by μCT data from BTX-induced muscle paralysis model shown in Figure 5c.

claim: Piezo1/2 are required for embryonic bone development and adult bone mass maintenance by mechanical forces.
source: Taken together, Piezo1/2 are required for embryonic bone development and adult bone mass maintenance by mechanical forces.
evidence: Inferred from limb explant culture and BTX-induced muscle paralysis experiments.

claim: Ctnnb1 and Yap1/Wwtr1 protein levels are reduced in bones of Prrx1-Cre-driven Piezo1 CKO and Piezo1/2 DKO mutants at P0.
source: We found that Ctnnb1 and Yap1/Wwtr1 protein levels were both reduced in the bones of Prrx1-Cre-driven Piezo1 CKO and Piezo1/2 DKO mutants at P0 and more reduction was found in the Piezo 1/2 DKO bone samples (Figure 6a,b, Figure 6—source data 1).
evidence: Supported by immunostaining and Western blot data shown in Figure 6a,b.

claim: Expression of Ctgf/Cyr61 and Tcf7/Lef1 is down-regulated in Piezo1 CKO and Piezo1/2 DKO mutant bones.
source: In addition, by qRT-PCR analysis, we found that expression of transcriptional targets of both Yap1/Wwtr1 and Wnt/Ctnnb1 such as Ctgf (Ccn2)/Cyr61(Ccn1) and Tcf7/Lef1, respectively, were down-regulated in the Piezo1 CKO and Piezo1/2 DKO mutant bones (Figure 6c, Figure 6—source data 1).
evidence: Supported by qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 6c.

claim: Ccn2 expression is reduced in developing humerus at E16.5 by removing Piezo1/2.
source: These results were further confirmed by in situ hybridization with a Ccn2 probe using the RNAscope technology (Figure 6d). Ccn2 expression was reduced in the developing humerus at E16.5 by removing Piezo1/2.
evidence: Supported by RNAscope in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 6d.

claim: Piezo1/2 activities may promote osteoblast differentiation by upregulating both Wnt/Ctnnb1 and Yap1 activities.
source: These results show that Piezo1/2 activities may promote osteoblast differentiation by upregulating both Wnt/Ctnnb1 and Yap1 activities.
evidence: Inferred from reduced Ctnnb1 and Yap1 protein levels and target gene expression in Piezo1/2 mutants.

claim: BMSCs express both Piezo1 and Piezo2, but Piezo1 expression is stronger.
source: The stiff surface of regular tissue culture dishes supports osteoblast differentiation of BMSCs, which expressed both Piezo1/2, but Piezo1 expression was stronger (Figure 6—figure supplement 1a).
evidence: Supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1a.

claim: Loss of Piezo1 or Piezo1/2 in BMSCs leads to reduced osteoblast differentiation.
source: However, loss of Piezo1 or Piezo1/2 by Cre Adenovirus (Ad-Cre) infection of the Piezo1f/f or Piezo1f/f; Piezo2f/f BMSCs (Figure 6—figure supplement 1a), respectively, led to reduced osteoblast differentiation and reduced Yap1/Wwtr1 and Wnt/Ctnnb1 signaling activities (Figure 6e, Figure 6—source data 1).
evidence: Supported by alkaline phosphatase staining and qPCR data shown in Figure 6e.

claim: Loss of Piezo1 or Piezo1/2 in BMSCs leads to reduced Yap1/Wwtr1 and Wnt/Ctnnb1 signaling activities.
source: However, loss of Piezo1 or Piezo1/2 by Cre Adenovirus (Ad-Cre) infection of the Piezo1f/f or Piezo1f/f; Piezo2f/f BMSCs (Figure 6—figure supplement 1a), respectively, led to reduced osteoblast differentiation and reduced Yap1/Wwtr1 and Wnt/Ctnnb1 signaling activities (Figure 6e, Figure 6—source data 1).
evidence: Supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 6e.

claim: Treating wild-type BMSCs with Yoda1 increases osteoblast differentiation.
source: Consistent with this, treating wild-type BMSCs with Yoda1 increased osteoblast differentiation as well as Wnt/Ctnnb1 and Yap1 transcriptional activities (Figure 6—figure supplement 1b, Figure 6—figure supplement 1—source data 1).
evidence: Supported by luciferase reporter assay data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1b.

claim: Treating wild-type BMSCs with Yoda1 increases Wnt/Ctnnb1 and Yap1 transcriptional activities.
source: Consistent with this, treating wild-type BMSCs with Yoda1 increased osteoblast differentiation as well as Wnt/Ctnnb1 and Yap1 transcriptional activities (Figure 6—figure supplement 1b, Figure 6—figure supplement 1—source data 1).
evidence: Supported by luciferase reporter assay data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1b.

claim: The osteogenic activity of Yoda1 is lost in the absence of Piezo1/2.
source: Such osteogenic activity of Yoda1 was lost in the absence of Piezo1/2 (Figure 6f, Figure 6—source data 1), suggesting that Yoda1 activity in promoting osteoblast differentiation depends on Piezo1.
evidence: Supported by alkaline phosphatase staining and qPCR data shown in Figure 6f.

claim: Yoda1 activity in promoting osteoblast differentiation depends on Piezo1.
source: Such osteogenic activity of Yoda1 was lost in the absence of Piezo1/2 (Figure 6f, Figure 6—source data 1), suggesting that Yoda1 activity in promoting osteoblast differentiation depends on Piezo1.
evidence: Inferred from loss of Yoda1 effect in Piezo1/2-deficient BMSCs.

claim: Blocking Ca2+ influx with Gd3+ blocks osteoblast differentiation similar to loss of Piezo1/2.
source: In addition, blocking Ca2+ influx with Gadolinium (Gd3+), a potent blocker of Calcium channels including the Piezos (Coste et al., 2010), blocked osteoblast differentiation similar to loss of Piezo1/2 (Figure 6f).
evidence: Supported by alkaline phosphatase staining and qPCR data shown in Figure 6f, and citation to previous work on Gd3+ as a calcium channel blocker.

claim: Piezo1/2 depend on Ca2+ influx and mediate mechanotransduction via Wnt/Ctnnb1 and Yap1 pathways in regulating osteoblast differentiation of BMSCs.
source: These results suggest that Piezo1/2 depend on Ca2+ influx and mediate mechanotransduction via the Wnt/Ctnnb1 and Yap1 pathways in regulating osteoblast differentiation of BMSCs.
evidence: Inferred from multiple experimental results showing effects of Piezo1/2 loss, Yoda1 treatment, and Gd3+ treatment on osteoblast differentiation and signaling pathways.

claim: Loss of Piezo1/2 completely abolishes the response of BMSCs to FSS in osteogenic assay.
source: We found that FSS stimulated osteoblast differentiation of wild-type BMSCs while loss of Piezo1/2 completely abolished the response of BMSC to FSS in the osteogenic assay (Figure 7a, Figure 7—source data 1).
evidence: Supported by alkaline phosphatase staining and qPCR data shown in Figure 7a.

claim: FSS upregulates protein levels of Ctnnb1 and Yap1 in BMSCs.
source: Importantly, FSS upregulated protein levels of Ctnnb1 and Yap1, while levels of phosphorylated Ctnnb1 and Yap1, which are cytoplasmic and destined for degradation, were reduced by FSS in BMSCs, indicating that FSS activated both Ctnnb1 and Yap1 activities (Figure 7b).
evidence: Supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 7b.

claim: FSS reduces levels of phosphorylated Ctnnb1 and Yap1 in BMSCs.
source: Importantly, FSS upregulated protein levels of Ctnnb1 and Yap1, while levels of phosphorylated Ctnnb1 and Yap1, which are cytoplasmic and destined for degradation, were reduced by FSS in BMSCs, indicating that FSS activated both Ctnnb1 and Yap1 activities (Figure 7b).
evidence: Supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 7b.

claim: FSS activates both Ctnnb1 and Yap1 activities in BMSCs.
source: Importantly, FSS upregulated protein levels of Ctnnb1 and Yap1, while levels of phosphorylated Ctnnb1 and Yap1, which are cytoplasmic and destined for degradation, were reduced by FSS in BMSCs, indicating that FSS activated both Ctnnb1 and Yap1 activities (Figure 7b).
evidence: Inferred from increased total protein and decreased phosphorylated forms of Ctnnb1 and Yap1 upon FSS treatment.

claim: Piezo1/2 loss in BMSCs abolishes osteogenic response to FSS.
source: Piezo1/2 loss in BMSCs abolished osteogenic response to FSS, reduced Ctnnb1 and Yap1 protein levels and increased Ctnnb1 and Yap1 phosphorylation (Figure 7a,b).
evidence: Supported by alkaline phosphatase staining, qPCR, and Western blot data shown in Figure 7a,b.

claim: Piezo1/2 loss in BMSCs reduces Ctnnb1 and Yap1 protein levels.
source: Piezo1/2 loss in BMSCs abolished osteogenic response to FSS, reduced Ctnnb1 and Yap1 protein levels and increased Ctnnb1 and Yap1 phosphorylation (Figure 7a,b).
evidence: Supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 7b.

claim: Piezo1/2 loss in BMSCs increases Ctnnb1 and Yap1 phosphorylation.
source: Piezo1/2 loss in BMSCs abolished osteogenic response to FSS, reduced Ctnnb1 and Yap1 protein levels and increased Ctnnb1 and Yap1 phosphorylation (Figure 7a,b).
evidence: Supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 7b.

claim: FSS-stimulated Yap1 activation may be independent of the Stk3/4 and Lats kinase cascade.
source: Interestingly, increased Yap1 phosphorylation was not accompanied by increase of phosphorylated and activated Stk4 (Mst1) or Lats1 kinases (Figure 7b), suggesting that FSS-stimulated Yap1 activation may be independent of the Stk3/4 and Lats kinase cascade that controls Yap1 phosphorylation in canonical Hippo signaling (Wu et al., 2003; Huang et al., 2005; Edgar, 2006; Pan, 2007).
evidence: Inferred from Western blot data showing no change in phosphorylated Stk4 or Lats1 upon FSS treatment, supported by citations to previous work on canonical Hippo signaling.

claim: Piezo1/2 are key mechanical force sensors that relay FSS signals to promote osteoblast differentiation through Yap1 and Ctnnb1 signaling.
source: These results suggest that Piezo1/2 are key mechanical force sensors that relay FSS signals to promote osteoblast differentiation through Yap1 and Ctnnb1 signaling.
evidence: Inferred from multiple experimental results showing effects of Piezo1/2 loss on FSS-induced osteoblast differentiation and signaling.

claim: Basal level Ca2+ signal is stronger in wild-type BMSCs compared with Piezo1/2 deficient BMSCs.
source: The basal level Ca2+ signal was stronger in the wild-type BMSCs compared with the Piezo1/2 deficient BMSCs (Figure 6c, Figure 6—source data 1).
evidence: Supported by calcium imaging data using GCaMP5G reporter shown in Figure 7c.

claim: FSS induces more robust Ca2+ influx in wild-type BMSCs compared to Piezo-deficient BMSCs.
source: More importantly, when BMSCs were subject to FSS, more robust Ca2+ influx was observed in the wild-type BMSCs compared to the Piezo-deficient ones (Figure 7c and Video 1).
evidence: Supported by calcium imaging data shown in Figure 7c and Video 1.

claim: Yoda1 treatment leads to more robust Ca2+ influx in wild-type BMSCs but not in Piezo1/2-deficient BMSCs.
source: Furthermore, Yoda1 treatment led to more robust Ca2+ influx in the wild type, but not Ad-Cre induced Piezo1/2-deficient BMSCs (Figure 7—figure supplement 1, Video 2, Figure 7—figure supplement 1—source data 1).
evidence: Supported by calcium imaging data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1 and Video 2.

claim: Piezo1/2 channels in BMSCs sense FSS-like mechanical forces to allow Ca2+ influx, leading to osteoblast differentiation.
source: These results together indicate that Piezo1/2 channels in BMSCs sense FSS-like mechanical forces to allow Ca2+ influx, leading to osteoblast differentiation.
evidence: Inferred from calcium imaging and osteoblast differentiation data.

claim: Wild-type BMSCs have difficulty spreading on a soft matrix (1 kPa) with diffused Yap1 localization.
source: While the wild-type BMSC have difficulty spreading on a soft matrix (1 kPa) with diffused Yap1 localization in both cytoplasmic and nuclear compartments, on a stiff matrix (40 kPa), they spread to much larger areas with strong nuclear Yap1 localization (Figure 8a).
evidence: Supported by immunostaining data on hydrogels shown in Figure 8a.

claim: Wild-type BMSCs spread to much larger areas with strong nuclear Yap1 localization on a stiff matrix (40 kPa).
source: While the wild-type BMSC have difficulty spreading on a soft matrix (1 kPa) with diffused Yap1 localization in both cytoplasmic and nuclear compartments, on a stiff matrix (40 kPa), they spread to much larger areas with strong nuclear Yap1 localization (Figure 8a).
evidence: Supported by immunostaining data on hydrogels shown in Figure 8a.

claim: Piezo1/2-deficient BMSCs plated on a stiff matrix behave more like wild-type BMSCs plated on a soft matrix.
source: Importantly, the Piezo1/2-deficient BMSCs plated on a stiff matrix behaved more like the wild-type BMSCs plated on a soft matrix. They showed weaker intracellular Ca2+ signaling (Figure 8—figure supplement 1, Figure 8—figure supplement 1—source data 1), were less spreading, contained less defined Yap1 nuclear localization (Figure 8a), and exhibited reduced Yap1 activities and osteoblast differentiation (Figure 8b).
evidence: Supported by calcium imaging, immunostaining, and osteoblast differentiation data shown in Figure 8a,b and Figure 8—figure supplement 1.

claim: Piezo1/2-deficient BMSCs show weaker intracellular Ca2+ signaling on stiff matrix.
source: Importantly, the Piezo1/2-deficient BMSCs plated on a stiff matrix behaved more like the wild-type BMSCs plated on a soft matrix. They showed weaker intracellular Ca2+ signaling (Figure 8—figure supplement 1, Figure 8—figure supplement 1—source data 1), were less spreading, contained less defined Yap1 nuclear localization (Figure 8a), and exhibited reduced Yap1 activities and osteoblast differentiation (Figure 8b).
evidence: Supported by calcium imaging data shown in Figure 8—figure supplement 1.

claim: Piezo1/2-deficient BMSCs are less spreading on stiff matrix.
source: Importantly, the Piezo1/2-deficient BMSCs plated on a stiff matrix behaved more like the wild-type BMSCs plated on a soft matrix. They showed weaker intracellular Ca2+ signaling (Figure 8—figure supplement 1, Figure 8—figure supplement 1—source data 1), were less spreading, contained less defined Yap1 nuclear localization (Figure 8a), and exhibited reduced Yap1 activities and osteoblast differentiation (Figure 8b).
evidence: Supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 8a.

claim: Piezo1/2-deficient BMSCs contain less defined Yap1 nuclear localization on stiff matrix.
source: Importantly, the Piezo1/2-deficient BMSCs plated on a stiff matrix behaved more like the wild-type BMSCs plated on a soft matrix. They showed weaker intracellular Ca2+ signaling (Figure 8—figure supplement 1, Figure 8—figure supplement 1—source data 1), were less spreading, contained less defined Yap1 nuclear localization (Figure 8a), and exhibited reduced Yap1 activities and osteoblast differentiation (Figure 8b).
evidence: Supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 8a.

claim: Piezo1/2-deficient BMSCs exhibit reduced Yap1 activities and osteoblast differentiation on stiff matrix.
source: Importantly, the Piezo1/2-deficient BMSCs plated on a stiff matrix behaved more like the wild-type BMSCs plated on a soft matrix. They showed weaker intracellular Ca2+ signaling (Figure 8—figure supplement 1, Figure 8—figure supplement 1—source data 1), were less spreading, contained less defined Yap1 nuclear localization (Figure 8a), and exhibited reduced Yap1 activities and osteoblast differentiation (Figure 8b).
evidence: Supported by alkaline phosphatase staining and qPCR data shown in Figure 8b.

claim: Piezo1/2 promote osteoblast differentiation by sensing matrix stiffness that regulates Yap1 nuclear localization.
source: These results indicate that Piezo1/2 also promote osteoblast differentiation by sensing matrix stiffness that is known to regulates Yap1 nuclear localization.
evidence: Inferred from experiments showing effects of Piezo1/2 loss on BMSC behavior on different stiffness matrices, supported by knowledge of matrix stiffness effects on Yap1.

claim: CsA treatment abolishes osteoblast differentiation enhanced by FSS.
source: CsA treatment abolished osteoblast differentiation as well as Yap1 and Ctnnb1 activation enhanced by FSS or Yoda1 treatment (Figure 8c,d, Figure 8—source data 1, Figure 6—figure supplement 1b, Figure 6—figure supplement 1—source data 1).
evidence: Supported by alkaline phosphatase staining and qPCR data shown in Figure 8c,d.

claim: CsA treatment abolishes Yap1 and Ctnnb1 activation enhanced by FSS.
source: CsA treatment abolished osteoblast differentiation as well as Yap1 and Ctnnb1 activation enhanced by FSS or Yoda1 treatment (Figure 8c,d, Figure 8—source data 1, Figure 6—figure supplement 1b, Figure 6—figure supplement 1—source data 1).
evidence: Supported by qPCR and luciferase reporter assay data shown in Figure 8c,d and Figure 6—figure supplement 1b.

claim: CsA treatment abolishes osteoblast differentiation enhanced by Yoda1 treatment.
source: CsA treatment abolished osteoblast differentiation as well as Yap1 and Ctnnb1 activation enhanced by FSS or Yoda1 treatment (Figure 8c,d, Figure 8—source data 1, Figure 6—figure supplement 1b, Figure 6—figure supplement 1—source data 1).
evidence: Supported by alkaline phosphatase staining and qPCR data shown in Figure 8d.

claim: CsA treatment abolishes Yap1 and Ctnnb1 activation enhanced by Yoda1 treatment.
source: CsA treatment abolished osteoblast differentiation as well as Yap1 and Ctnnb1 activation enhanced by FSS or Yoda1 treatment (Figure 8c,d, Figure 8—source data 1, Figure 6—figure supplement 1b, Figure 6—figure supplement 1—source data 1).
evidence: Supported by qPCR and luciferase reporter assay data shown in Figure 8d and Figure 6—figure supplement 1b.

claim: Ppp3ca may act downstream of Piezo1/2 in mechanotransduction to regulate Yap1 and Ctnnb1 activities during osteoblast differentiation.
source: These results suggest that Ppp3ca may act downstream of Piezo1/2 in mechanotransduction to regulate Yap1 and Ctnnb1 activities during osteoblast differentiation.
evidence: Inferred from CsA inhibition experiments showing loss of Yap1 and Ctnnb1 activation by FSS or Yoda1.

claim: Loss of Piezo1/2 together leads to a strong increase of Nfatc1 phosphorylation in developing bone.
source: We found that loss of Piezo1/2 together, led to a strong increase of Nfatc1 phosphorylation in the developing bone (Figure 9a, Figure 9—source data 1).
evidence: Supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 9a.

claim: Loss of Piezo1 alone increases Nfatc1 phosphorylation, although to a lesser extent than Piezo1/2 loss.
source: Loss of Piezo1 alone also increased Nfatc1 phosphorylation, although to a lesser extent (Figure 9a).
evidence: Supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 9a.

claim: Piezo1/2 activate Nfatc1 by inhibiting its phosphorylation in developing bone.
source: As Nfat transcription factors are highly phosphorylated and cytoplasmic in unstimulated cells, and an increase in intracellular Ca2+ leads to Nfatc1 dephosphorylation by Ppp3ca and its subsequent nuclear translocation to activate downstream gene expression (Liu et al., 1997; Masuda et al., 1997; Beals et al., 1997; Crabtree and Olson, 2002), these results suggest that Piezo1/2 activate Nfatc1 by inhibiting its phosphorylation in the developing bone.
evidence: Inferred from increased Nfatc1 phosphorylation in Piezo1/2 mutants, supported by citations to previous work on NFAT regulation.

claim: Yoda1 treatment stimulates transcription activities of NFAT, YAP1, and CTNNB1 in HEK293T cells.
source: Yoda1 treatment stimulated transcription activities of not only NFAT, but also YAP1 and CTNNB1, all of which were abolished by knocking down PIEZO1 (Figure 9b).
evidence: Supported by luciferase reporter assay data shown in Figure 9b.

claim: Knocking down PIEZO1 abolishes Yoda1-stimulated transcription activities of NFAT, YAP1, and CTNNB1.
source: Yoda1 treatment stimulated transcription activities of not only NFAT, but also YAP1 and CTNNB1, all of which were abolished by knocking down PIEZO1 (Figure 9b).
evidence: Supported by luciferase reporter assay data shown in Figure 9b.

claim: Activation of PIEZO1 upregulates NFATc1, YAP1, and CTNNB1 transcriptional activities.
source: These results indicate that activation of PIEZO1 upregulates NFATc1, YAP1 or CTNNB1 transcriptional activities.
evidence: Inferred from luciferase reporter assay results showing Yoda1 effects.

claim: Transcriptional activities of NFAT, YAP1, and CTNNB1 are mutually enhanced, with the exception that YAP1 does not enhance NFAT activities in HEK293T cells.
source: Indeed, transcriptional activities of NFAT, YAP1 and CTNNB1 were mutually enhanced, with the only exception that YAP1 did not seem to enhance NFAT activities in HEK293T cells (Figure 9—figure supplement 1b, Figure 9—figure supplement 1—source data 1).
evidence: Supported by luciferase reporter assay data shown in Figure 9—figure supplement 1b.

claim: YAP1 and NFATc1 interaction is promoted by FSS or Yoda1 treatment.
source: To further understand the mechanism underlying YAP1 and CTNNB1 activation in concert with NFATc1, we first tested YAP1 and NFATc1 interaction by co-immunoprecipitation (Co-IP) assays and found such interaction was promoted by FSS or Yoda1 treatment, but inhibited by CsA or Gd3+ treatment (Figure 9c, Figure 9—source data 1, Figure 9—figure supplement 1b, Figure 9—figure supplement 1—source data 1).
evidence: Supported by co-immunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 9c and Figure 9—figure supplement 1b.

claim: YAP1 and NFATc1 interaction is inhibited by CsA or Gd3+ treatment.
source: To further understand the mechanism underlying YAP1 and CTNNB1 activation in concert with NFATc1, we first tested YAP1 and NFATc1 interaction by co-immunoprecipitation (Co-IP) assays and found such interaction was promoted by FSS or Yoda1 treatment, but inhibited by CsA or Gd3+ treatment (Figure 9c, Figure 9—source data 1, Figure 9—figure supplement 1b, Figure 9—figure supplement 1—source data 1).
evidence: Supported by co-immunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 9c and Figure 9—figure supplement 1b.

claim: PIEZO1-induced Ca2+ signaling promotes NFATc1 interaction with YAP1.
source: These results suggest that PIEZO1-induced Ca2+ signaling promoted NFATc1 interaction with YAP1.
evidence: Inferred from co-immunoprecipitation results showing effects of Yoda1, FSS, CsA, and Gd3+ on NFATc1-YAP1 interaction.

claim: NFATc1 and YAP1 nuclear localization are both robustly promoted by FSS in HEK293 cells.
source: To further confirm that PIEZO1 may activate YAP1 by activating PPP3CA and NFATc1, we examined NFATc1 and YAP1 nuclear localization in HEK293 cells and found that both were robustly promoted by FSS (Figure 9d).
evidence: Supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 9d.

claim: Overexpression of PPP3CA promotes YAP1 dephosphorylation.
source: In addition, overexpression of the catalytic subunit of PPP3CA promoted YAP1 dephosphorylation (Figure 9—figure supplement 1c, Figure 9—figure supplement 1—source data 1).
evidence: Supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 9—figure supplement 1c.

claim: Yoda1 treatment mimics the effects of FSS treatment or PPP3CA expression on YAP1 and NFATc1 nuclear localization.
source: Moreover, Yoda1 treatment mimicked the effects of FSS treatment or PPP3CA expression (Figure 9e, Figure 9—figure supplement 1c).
evidence: Supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 9e and Western blot data in Figure 9—figure supplement 1c.

claim: Gd3+ treatment inhibits nuclear localization of NFATc1 and YAP1 induced by FSS or Yoda1 treatment.
source: Blocking Ca2+ influx with Gd3+ treatment or PPP3CA activity with CsA treatment both inhibited nuclear localization of NFATc1 and YAP1 induced by FSS or Yoda1 treatment (Figure 9e).
evidence: Supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 9e.

claim: CsA treatment inhibits nuclear localization of NFATc1 and YAP1 induced by FSS or Yoda1 treatment.
source: Blocking Ca2+ influx with Gd3+ treatment or PPP3CA activity with CsA treatment both inhibited nuclear localization of NFATc1 and YAP1 induced by FSS or Yoda1 treatment (Figure 9e).
evidence: Supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 9e.

claim: NFATc1 interaction with YAP1 or CTNNB1 is synergistically promoted by the presence of all three transcription factors.
source: Furthermore, NFATc1 interaction with YAP1 or CTNNB1 was synergistically promoted by the other, as presence of all three transcription factors robustly increased their interactions (Figure 9—figure supplement 1d, Figure 9—figure supplement 1—source data 1).
evidence: Supported by co-immunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 9—figure supplement 1d.

claim: Yoda1 treatment quickly reduces Yap1 and Ctnnb1 phosphorylation in mouse primary BMSCs.
source: We therefore tested whether the Piezo1-mediated mechanotransduction promotes osteoblast differentiation by a concerted dephosphorylation of endogenous Yap1 and Ctnnb1 in mouse primary BMSCs. Indeed, Yoda 1 treatment quickly reduced Yap1 and Ctnnb1 phosphorylation (Figure 9f).
evidence: Supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 9f.

claim: Yoda1 activity in reducing Yap1 and Ctnnb1 phosphorylation is abolished in Piezo1/2-deficient BMSCs.
source: Such activity of Yoda1 was abolished in the Piezo1/2-deficient BMSCs (Figure 9—figure supplement 1e).
evidence: Supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 9—figure supplement 1e.

claim: Gd3+ treatment promotes Yap1 and Ctnnb1 phosphorylation while reducing their protein levels within 30 min.
source: Conversely, blocking Ca2+ influx by Gd3+ treatment promoted Yap1 and Ctnnb1 phosphorylation while reducing their protein levels within 30 min (Figure 9—figure supplement 1f).
evidence: Supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 9—figure supplement 1f.

claim: Ppp3ca binds to Nfatc1, Yap1, and Ctnnb1 in mouse primary BMSCs.
source: Furthermore, in the mouse primary BMSCs, Ppp3ca was found to bind not only Nfatc1, but also Yap1 and Ctnnb1. These interactions were enhanced by Yoda1 treatment and inhibited by CsA (Figure 9g, Figure 9—source data 1).
evidence: Supported by co-immunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 9g.

claim: Ppp3ca binding to Nfatc1, Yap1, and Ctnnb1 is enhanced by Yoda1 treatment.
source: Furthermore, in the mouse primary BMSCs, Ppp3ca was found to bind not only Nfatc1, but also Yap1 and Ctnnb1. These interactions were enhanced by Yoda1 treatment and inhibited by CsA (Figure 9g, Figure 9—source data 1).
evidence: Supported by co-immunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 9g.

claim: Ppp3ca binding to Nfatc1, Yap1, and Ctnnb1 is inhibited by CsA.
source: Furthermore, in the mouse primary BMSCs, Ppp3ca was found to bind not only Nfatc1, but also Yap1 and Ctnnb1. These interactions were enhanced by Yoda1 treatment and inhibited by CsA (Figure 9g, Figure 9—source data 1).
evidence: Supported by co-immunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 9g.

claim: Ca2+/Ppp3ca signaling activated by Piezo1 leads to concerted activation of Yap1 and Ctnnb1 with Nfat to promote osteoblast differentiation and bone formation.
source: Taken together, our data indicate that Ca2+/Ppp3ca signaling activated by Piezo1 leads to concerted activation of Yap1 and Ctnnb1 with Nfat, all of which act together to regulate transcription changes that promote osteoblast differentiation and bone formation.
evidence: Inferred from multiple experimental results showing Piezo1-dependent Ca2+ signaling, Ppp3ca interactions, and transcription factor activation.

claim: BIO treatment increases long bone length in Piezo1/2 DKO mice.
source: We found that BIO treatment increased long bone length and bone mass with reduced bone fractures in the Piezo1/2 DKO mice (Figure 10a, Figure 10—source data 1, Figure 10—figure supplement 1a,b).
evidence: Supported by skeletal staining and μCT data shown in Figure 10a and Figure 10—figure supplement 1a,b.

claim: BIO treatment increases bone mass in Piezo1/2 DKO mice.
source: We found that BIO treatment increased long bone length and bone mass with reduced bone fractures in the Piezo1/2 DKO mice (Figure 10a, Figure 10—source data 1, Figure 10—figure supplement 1a,b).
evidence: Supported by μCT data shown in Figure 10a.

claim: BIO treatment reduces bone fractures in Piezo1/2 DKO mice.
source: We found that BIO treatment increased long bone length and bone mass with reduced bone fractures in the Piezo1/2 DKO mice (Figure 10a, Figure 10—source data 1, Figure 10—figure supplement 1a,b).
evidence: Supported by skeletal staining data shown in Figure 10—figure supplement 1a.

claim: BIO treatment enhances Sp7 and Spp1 expression while reducing Ctsk expression.
source: Further analyses showed that BIO treatment enhanced Sp7 and Spp1 expression while Ctsk expression was reduced (Figure 10b).
evidence: Supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 10b.

claim: Increased Ctnnb1 activities enhance osteoblast differentiation and maturation while inhibiting osteoclast differentiation.
source: Thus, increased Ctnnb1 activities enhanced osteoblast differentiation and maturation while osteoclast differentiation was inhibited.
evidence: Inferred from BIO treatment effects on Sp7, Spp1, and Ctsk expression.

claim: BIO treatment increases Ctnnb1 protein levels and reduces Ctnnb1 phosphorylation in BMSCs.
source: To test whether Ctnnb1 and Yap1 also enhances each other's activity in BMSCs, we treated the BMSCs with BIO or XMU-MP-1, an inhibitor of Hippo kinase Stk3/4 (Fan et al., 2016), and found that while BIO increased Ctnnb1 protein levels and reduced Ctnnb1 phosphorylation as expected, it also increased Yap1 protein levels and reduced Yap1 phosphorylation (Figure 10—figure supplement 1c).
evidence: Supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 10—figure supplement 1c.

claim: BIO treatment increases Yap1 protein levels and reduces Yap1 phosphorylation in BMSCs.
source: To test whether Ctnnb1 and Yap1 also enhances each other's activity in BMSCs, we treated the BMSCs with BIO or XMU-MP-1, an inhibitor of Hippo kinase Stk3/4 (Fan et al., 2016), and found that while BIO increased Ctnnb1 protein levels and reduced Ctnnb1 phosphorylation as expected, it also increased Yap1 protein levels and reduced Yap1 phosphorylation (Figure 10—figure supplement 1c).
evidence: Supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 10—figure supplement 1c.

claim: XMU-MP-1 treatment reduces Yap1 phosphorylation and increases total and non-phosphorylated Ctnnb1 protein levels in BMSCs.
source: Likewise, reduction of Yap1 phosphorylation caused by XMU-MP-1 treatment was also accompanied by increase in total and non-phosphorylated Ctnnb1 protein levels.
evidence: Inferred from Western blot data.

claim: Verteporfin reduces the effects of BIO in promoting both Ctnnb1 and Yap1 levels.
source: In addition, blocking Yap1 transcription activity by Verteporfin (VP) (Liu-Chittenden et al., 2012) reduced the effects of BIO in promoting both Ctnnb1 and Yap1 levels, suggesting that Ctnnb1 requires Yap1 activity to be fully upregulated (Figure 10—figure supplement 1c).
evidence: Supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 10—figure supplement 1c and citation to previous work on Verteporfin.

claim: Ctnnb1 requires Yap1 activity to be fully upregulated.
source: In addition, blocking Yap1 transcription activity by Verteporfin (VP) (Liu-Chittenden et al., 2012) reduced the effects of BIO in promoting both Ctnnb1 and Yap1 levels, suggesting that Ctnnb1 requires Yap1 activity to be fully upregulated (Figure 10—figure supplement 1c).
evidence: Inferred from Verteporfin inhibition experiments.

claim: BIO treatment partially rescues reduction of osteoblast differentiation due to Piezo1/2 loss in BMSCs in vitro.
source: Consistently, BIO treatment of BMSCs in vitro partially rescued reduction of osteoblast differentiation due to Piezo1/2 loss (Figure 10—figure supplement 1d).
evidence: Supported by alkaline phosphatase staining and qPCR data shown in Figure 10—figure supplement 1d.

claim: BIO treatment increases Ctnnb1 protein levels but the increase of Yap1 is less appreciable in Piezo1/2 mutant bones.
source: However, while Ctnnb1 protein levels were increased by BIO treatment, the increase of Yap1 was less appreciable (Figure 10c), suggesting that while Ctnnb1 activation is essential for osteoblast differentiation and can promote Yap1 activation, Yap1 is also regulated by Piezo1/2 by Ctnnb1-independent pathways and it is the concerted activation of NFATc1, Yap1 and Ctnnb1 that constitutes a fully functional mechanotransduction pathway downstream of Piezo channels in promoting bone formation.
evidence: Supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 10c.

claim: Ctnnb1 activation is essential for osteoblast differentiation and can promote Yap1 activation.
source: However, while Ctnnb1 protein levels were increased by BIO treatment, the increase of Yap1 was less appreciable (Figure 10c), suggesting that while Ctnnb1 activation is essential for osteoblast differentiation and can promote Yap1 activation, Yap1 is also regulated by Piezo1/2 by Ctnnb1-independent pathways and it is the concerted activation of NFATc1, Yap1 and Ctnnb1 that constitutes a fully functional mechanotransduction pathway downstream of Piezo channels in promoting bone formation.
evidence: Inferred from BIO rescue experiments and differential effects on Ctnnb1 and Yap1.

claim: Yap1 is regulated by Piezo1/2 by Ctnnb1-independent pathways.
source: However, while Ctnnb1 protein levels were increased by BIO treatment, the increase of Yap1 was less appreciable (Figure 10c), suggesting that while Ctnnb1 activation is essential for osteoblast differentiation and can promote Yap1 activation, Yap1 is also regulated by Piezo1/2 by Ctnnb1-independent pathways and it is the concerted activation of NFATc1, Yap1 and Ctnnb1 that constitutes a fully functional mechanotransduction pathway downstream of Piezo channels in promoting bone formation.
evidence: Inferred from incomplete rescue of Yap1 levels by BIO treatment.

claim: Concerted activation of NFATc1, Yap1, and Ctnnb1 constitutes a fully functional mechanotransduction pathway downstream of Piezo channels in promoting bone formation.
source: However, while Ctnnb1 protein levels were increased by BIO treatment, the increase of Yap1 was less appreciable (Figure 10c), suggesting that while Ctnnb1 activation is essential for osteoblast differentiation and can promote Yap1 activation, Yap1 is also regulated by Piezo1/2 by Ctnnb1-independent pathways and it is the concerted activation of NFATc1, Yap1 and Ctnnb1 that constitutes a fully functional mechanotransduction pathway downstream of Piezo channels in promoting bone formation.
evidence: Inferred from multiple experimental results showing interactions and mutual regulation of NFATc1, Yap1, and Ctnnb1.

claim: PIEZO1 and PIEZO2 expression in human BMSCs shows a significant negative correlation with age.
source: In our preliminary study, expression of PIEZO1 and PIEZO2 in human BMSCs obtained from 11 male subjects showed a significant negative correlation with age (Figure 11, Figure 11—source data 1), suggesting that reduction of PIEZO channels might also contribute to bone aging.
evidence: Supported by qRT-PCR data from human BMSCs shown in Figure 11.

claim: Reduction of PIEZO channels might contribute to bone aging.
source: In our preliminary study, expression of PIEZO1 and PIEZO2 in human BMSCs obtained from 11 male subjects showed a significant negative correlation with age (Figure 11, Figure 11—source data 1), suggesting that reduction of PIEZO channels might also contribute to bone aging.
evidence: Inferred from negative correlation between PIEZO expression and age in human BMSCs.

claim: Piezo1 and Piezo2 are mechanosensitive channels required for bone development and osteoblast differentiation.
source: Here, we identified the mechanosensitive channels Piezo1 and Piezo2 as key force sensors required for bone development and osteoblast differentiation.
evidence: Supported by multiple experimental results throughout the study.

claim: Loss of Piezo1 in mesenchymal or osteoblast progenitor cells leads to multiple spontaneous bone fractures in newborn mice.
source: Loss of Piezo1, or more severely Piezo1/2, in mesenchymal or osteoblast progenitor cells, led to multiple spontaneous bone fractures in newborn mice due to inhibition of osteoblast differentiation and increased bone resorption.
evidence: Supported by skeletal staining and histological analyses.

claim: Loss of Piezo1/2 in mesenchymal or osteoblast progenitor cells leads to more severe spontaneous bone fractures in newborn mice than loss of Piezo1 alone.
source: Loss of Piezo1, or more severely Piezo1/2, in mesenchymal or osteoblast progenitor cells, led to multiple spontaneous bone fractures in newborn mice due to inhibition of osteoblast differentiation and increased bone resorption.
evidence: Supported by skeletal staining and histological analyses.

claim: Loss of Piezo1/2 renders mice resistant to further bone loss caused by unloading in both bone development and homeostasis.
source: In addition, loss of Piezo1/2 rendered resistant to further bone loss caused by unloading in both bone development and homeostasis.
evidence: Supported by limb explant culture and BTX-induced muscle paralysis experiments.

claim: Piezo1/2 relay fluid shear stress and extracellular matrix stiffness signals to activate Ca2+ influx.
source: Mechanistically, Piezo1/2 relayed fluid shear stress and extracellular matrix stiffness signals to activate Ca2+ influx to stimulate Calcineurin, which promotes concerted activation of NFATc1, YAP1 and ß-catenin transcription factors by inducing their dephosphorylation as well as NFAT/YAP1/ß-catenin complex formation.
evidence: Supported by calcium imaging, FSS experiments, and hydrogel experiments.

claim: Piezo1/2-activated Ca2+ influx stimulates Calcineurin.
source: Mechanistically, Piezo1/2 relayed fluid shear stress and extracellular matrix stiffness signals to activate Ca2+ influx to stimulate Calcineurin, which promotes concerted activation of NFATc1, YAP1 and ß-catenin transcription factors by inducing their dephosphorylation as well as NFAT/YAP1/ß-catenin complex formation.
evidence: Supported by CsA inhibition experiments and co-immunoprecipitation data.

claim: Calcineurin promotes concerted activation of NFATc1, YAP1, and ß-catenin by inducing their dephosphorylation.
source: Mechanistically, Piezo1/2 relayed fluid shear stress and extracellular matrix stiffness signals to activate Ca2+ influx to stimulate Calcineurin, which promotes concerted activation of NFATc1, YAP1 and ß-catenin transcription factors by inducing their dephosphorylation as well as NFAT/YAP1/ß-catenin complex formation.
evidence: Supported by Western blot data showing reduced phosphorylation of NFATc1, YAP1, and ß-catenin upon Piezo1 activation.

claim: Calcineurin promotes NFAT/YAP1/ß-catenin complex formation.
source: Mechanistically, Piezo1/2 relayed fluid shear stress and extracellular matrix stiffness signals to activate Ca2+ influx to stimulate Calcineurin, which promotes concerted activation of NFATc1, YAP1 and ß-catenin transcription factors by inducing their dephosphorylation as well as NFAT/YAP1/ß-catenin complex formation.
evidence: Supported by co-immunoprecipitation data showing interactions between NFATc1, YAP1, and ß-catenin.

claim: Yap1 and ß-catenin activities are reduced in Piezo1 and Piezo1/2 mutant bones.
source: Yap1 and ß-catenin activities were reduced in the Piezo1 and Piezo1/2 mutant bones and such defects were partially rescued by enhanced ß-catenin activities.
evidence: Supported by immunostaining, Western blot, and qPCR data.

claim: Defects in Yap1 and ß-catenin activities in Piezo1 and Piezo1/2 mutant bones are partially rescued by enhanced ß-catenin activities.
source: Yap1 and ß-catenin activities were reduced in the Piezo1 and Piezo1/2 mutant bones and such defects were partially rescued by enhanced ß-catenin activities.
evidence: Supported by BIO treatment experiments showing partial rescue of bone phenotypes.
